title: Back of the Envelope
summary: Turn daily users into requests per second, servers, storage and bandwidth — in five minutes, with round numbers.

goals.text: Turn daily users into requests per second
Size for the peak, not the average

steps.title: Will it fit — before you build it?
body: Snapgrain, a photo-journal app, is planning its launch. The investors ask: how many servers? How much storage? How much bandwidth? Nobody can know exactly — but you can get within a factor of two in five minutes.
That's a back-of-the-envelope estimate: round every number, multiply, and keep the units honest. The goal is the right order of magnitude, not three decimal places.

callout.text: Estimates exist to make decisions: one database or fifty? A CDN or not? You only need enough precision to choose.

steps.title: From users to requests per second
body: Start with daily active users (DAU). Snapgrain expects 10 million. A typical user opens the app a few times and makes about 40 requests a day — feeds, likes, a post now and then.
10M × 40 = 400 million requests a day. A day has 86,400 seconds — call it 10⁵ — so the average is about 4,600 requests per second.

callout.text: Handy shortcut: 1 million requests a day ≈ 12 per second.

steps.title: Nobody uses an app on average
body: Traffic follows the sun: quiet at 4 a.m., busiest in the evening, with spikes when a post goes viral. You must survive the peak, not the average.
A common rule of thumb for consumer apps is peak ≈ 2–3× the average (more for launches and sales). Using 3×: about 14,000 requests per second.

steps.title: Divide by what one machine can do
body: Next, one server's capacity. Say a request costs ~5 ms of CPU: one core handles 200 per second, an 8-core server 1,600. Planning to run at ~60% busy, to stay off the latency knee, leaves ~1,000 req/s per server.
14,000 ÷ 1,000 = 14 servers for the peak. Add two spares so a crash or a deploy doesn't overload the rest: 16 servers.
changes: ~ Peak divided by safe per-server capacity

steps.title: What piles up every day
body: Storage grows with what users create. If half of them post one photo a day, that's 5 million photos. At ~300 KB each (compressed, plus a thumbnail) that's 1.5 TB a day.
Over a year: 1.5 TB × 365 ≈ 550 TB. The metadata — caption, owner, timestamps, ~1 KB per photo — adds only 5 GB a day, under 2 TB a year. The bytes are in the photos.

callout.text: Durable storage keeps copies. With 3 replicas, 550 TB of photos needs about 1.6 PB of raw disk.

steps.title: Reading is heavier than writing
body: Each user scrolls past about 100 photos a day. Served at ~150 KB (a screen-sized version), that's 10M × 100 × 150 KB = 150 TB leaving Snapgrain every day.
150 TB ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1.7 GB/s — about 14 Gbit/s on average and ~40 Gbit/s at a 3× peak. That number, more than the server count, says Snapgrain will want a CDN.
changes: + Photo downloads flowing back to users

steps.title: Numbers worth remembering
body: Estimates go quickly when a few anchors live in your head. Powers of ten turn multiplication into counting zeros; rough latency numbers tell you which operations you can afford inside a single request.

Read from main memory~100 ns
Random read from SSD~100 µs
Round trip inside a data centre~0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD~1 ms
Round trip across an ocean~80–150 ms

callout.text: Memory is ~1,000× faster than SSD, which is ~1,000× faster than a cross-ocean round trip. A few of those per request is fine; thousands is not.

steps.title: Good enough — and knowing why
body: Every input could be off by 2×: maybe users make 80 requests a day, maybe photos average 500 KB. That's fine. The estimate's job is to show which problems are big (egress, photo storage) and which are small (metadata, a modest web tier).
Write the assumptions next to the result. When real traffic arrives, swap in measured numbers and the same arithmetic tells you what to change.

callout.text: If two designs differ by 10× in the estimate, the estimate decides. If they differ by 20%, go and measure.

steps.title: Estimating on one page
body:
• DAU × requests per user ÷ ~10⁵ s = average req/s; multiply by 2–3 for the peak.
  • Servers = peak ÷ safe per-server capacity, plus spares.
  • Storage per year = items per day × size × 365 (× replicas).
  • Bandwidth = reads × size — often the biggest number of all.
  • Round hard, write assumptions down, and look for the term that dominates.
